transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I, uh... well, my wife really pushed me to come in. We've been married for thirty-two years, and she's always been the organized one, you know? Keeping track of everything. Lately, though, it's become a real point of contention between us. See, my cousin, he's been having some health issues—nothing too serious, just some mobility things, but he needs help getting to his various appointments. So my wife, bless her heart, she coordinates with his daughter about who is driving him on what day. And she'll be standing right there in the kitchen, making a cup of coffee, and she'll be telling me all about the schedule for the week. "We need to pick up Dave on Tuesday at 2:00, and then Thursday his daughter has him," that sort of thing. And I'm standing right there. I'm looking right at her. I can see her lips moving, I hear the sound of her voice, I'm nodding along... and then a minute later, she'll ask me to confirm the time, and I realize I didn't actually take in half of what she just said. It's like the words just bounced right off my forehead. And she gets so frustrated, understandably so, because she thinks I'm just ignoring her or that I don't care about my cousin, which isn't true at all! I just... I don't know where my brain goes in those moments. It's like I'm tuned to the wrong radio station, even though I'm staring right at the broadcaster. So, anyway, that's the main thing that finally got me to make this appointment. She said I need to get my hearing checked or my head checked, and my hearing is fine, so here I am.
Looking back, have you had trouble tuning in and paying attention your whole life, including when you were a kid, or is this a newer change for you?

Well, you know, it is funny you ask that, because my wife actually brought up the exact same thing when we were arguing about my cousin's driving schedule. She asked if I had always been like this, just sort of drifting off. And it really got me thinking back, way back. I am talking way back to when I was just a little guy, definitely before I was twelve years old. 

I remember being in grade school... maybe third or fourth grade? We had those old wooden desks, the ones where the top lifts up on a little metal hinge, you know the kind I mean? You would keep all your heavy textbooks and your pencil boxes in there. And I remember parent-teacher conferences were always a whole ordeal in our house. My mother would come home—she was a very practical, no-nonsense woman, my mother—and she would sit me down at the kitchen table. And she would relay exactly what the teachers had said. It was always the exact same story, year after year. They would tell my parents that I was a bright boy, that I had a lot of potential, but then the other shoe would always drop. They told them I was always daydreaming. Just staring out the window, completely lost in my own little world while everyone else was doing their lessons. 

And that desk I mentioned, it was like a black hole. I would actually do my homework at home, I really would, but then the next day I would just leave it sitting right there inside my desk instead of walking up to the front of the room and turning it in. Or we would be doing a worksheet right there in the middle of class, and I would get through the first three questions, and then my mind would just wander off to what I was going to do at recess, or a comic book I had read. The teacher would constantly have to come over, tap on my shoulder, and give me reminders to actually finish my classwork. 

So, it is definitely not a new change at all. It has just always been this way, I suppose, ever since I was a kid. I guess I just managed to get by for a long time, or maybe my wife just picked up the slack for the last thirty years and is finally tired of it, but the whole tuning out thing... yeah, that goes way, way back.
Growing up or even now, have you ever struggled with physical restlessness, like feeling constantly on the go or needing to fidget, or were you mostly calm and quiet?

No, no, not at all. That really doesn't sound like me. I've never been the type to bounce off the walls or anything like that. Even when I was a kid, you know, my brother—my older brother, Tom—he was the one who couldn't sit still. He'd be running around the yard, climbing the oak tree out back, constantly scraping his knees. My mother was always chasing after him with a band-aid and a wet washcloth. But me? I was perfectly content to just sit in the living room on the rug with a book or my toy cars. I could sit there for hours, just, you know, completely still, in my own head. 

And even now, I don't really get that feeling of needing to move or fidget. When my wife and I watch television in the evenings—we usually watch those British detective shows, she loves those, the ones with the little villages where everyone seems to be a murderer—I'll just sit in my recliner. I'm perfectly relaxed. I might drift off and miss the entire plot of the episode, mind you, and then she has to explain to me who killed the vicar and why, but my body is completely still. I don't tap my feet, I don't drum my fingers on the armrest, nothing like that. I'm usually just... very calm, physically speaking. It's really just my mind that seems to be, well, floating away from whatever is right in front of me. So, no, the physical restlessness, the feeling like I have a motor running inside me... I've never really experienced that, not as a boy and not now at fifty-nine.
